slides.title: Room 6: Roles
slides.narration: Welcome to Lesson 11. This room is about roles. It is where two people can use the same words and picture completely different marriages.

slides.quote: “Submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ. … Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her … let each one of you love his wife as himself, and let the wife see that she respects her husband.”
slides.narration:
Let’s begin with Scripture. Ephesians chapter 5, verses 21 to 33. We will read the whole passage, because it should be read whole.

“Submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ. Wives, submit to your own husbands, as to the Lord. For the husband is the head of the wife even as Christ is the head of the church, his body, and is himself its Savior. Now as the church submits to Christ, so also wives should submit in everything to their husbands. Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her, that he might sanctify her, having cleansed her by the washing of water with the word, so that he might present the church to himself in splendor, without spot or wrinkle or any such thing, that she might be holy and without blemish. In the same way husbands should love their wives as their own bodies. He who loves his wife loves himself. For no one ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the church, because we are members of his body. ‘Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh.’ This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church. However, let each one of you love his wife as himself, and let the wife see that she respects her husband.”

slides.title: Verse 21 comes first
body: “Submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ.” Paul speaks to every person in the household: wives, husbands, children, parents, bondservants and masters.
slides.narration:
This is one of the most discussed passages in the Bible, so let’s go carefully.

Start with how it opens. Verse 21 immediately precedes the instructions to wives and husbands: “submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ.” Christians agree that it matters for reading what follows, though they differ over precisely how it shapes the distinct instructions to wives and husbands. The section is about conduct inside a Christian household. It speaks here to wives and husbands, and as the household teaching continues into chapter 6, Paul also addresses children, parents, bondservants and masters. Every person in the household is spoken to.

slides.title: Christ’s self-giving love
body: “As Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her.” A picture of nourishing and cherishing. Sacrifice, not command.
slides.narration: Now look at what is said to husbands. Paul gives husbands an extended command centred on Christ’s self-giving love: “as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her.” That is a picture of costly love. It is a picture of nourishing and cherishing. The husband’s calling here is to sacrifice, not to command.

slides.title: Both are named
body: “Let each one of you love his wife as himself, and let the wife see that she respects her husband.” Both are meant to be lived.
slides.narration: And notice the end. “Let each one of you love his wife as himself, and let the wife see that she respects her husband.” Love and respect. Both are named, and both are meant to be lived.

slides.title: This lesson will not choose for you
body: Some hear a husband’s distinct responsibility for leadership. Others read the opening verse as setting the tone of mutual submission.
slides.narration: I want to be honest about one thing: this passage has been read in different ways by serious Christians. Some hear it as describing a husband’s distinct responsibility for leadership. Others read the opening verse as setting the tone for mutual submission throughout. This lesson will not tell you which to choose. Our task is different, and it is one the passage itself supports.

slides.title: Scripture is never given to silence anyone
body: Whatever position you reach, this passage permits neither selfish authority nor careless treatment.
slides.narration: Here is the truth this lesson stands on. Whatever position you reach about marital roles, this passage permits neither selfish authority nor careless treatment. Husbands are called to Christlike, self-giving love, and wives are addressed as responsible disciples whose response is offered in reverence for Christ. And Scripture is never given to us to silence anyone.

slides.kicker: The problem the passage cannot solve
slides.title: Same phrase, different marriages
body: Two people can agree on “biblical roles” and picture completely different marriages. The work is to say, in plain words, what you mean.
slides.narration: That brings us to a problem the passage cannot solve for you. Two people can agree perfectly on the phrase “biblical roles” and still picture two completely different marriages. So the work of this lesson is to say, in plain words, what you actually mean.

slides.kicker: Here is how it goes wrong
slides.title: Who has the final say?
body: It starts practically: who cooks, who pays the bills, who deals with the car. Then, unnoticed, it becomes: who has the final say? They are different subjects.
slides.narration:
Here is how it usually goes wrong.

The conversation starts practically. Who cooks, who pays the bills, who handles the children, who deals with the car. Then, without anyone noticing, it becomes a different question: who has the final say? That is not the same subject, and the two need to be separated before either can be settled.

slides.title: Headship. Submission. Partnership.
body: Each word means different things to different people. Do not assume the same vocabulary means the same marriage.
slides.narration: And the vocabulary hides the disagreement. One person hears “headship” and understands: the husband carries a particular responsibility for the family, and should lead sacrificially. Another hears: the husband gets the final decision whenever we disagree. Those are not the same thing. One hears “submission” and thinks: I willingly respect and support my husband’s leadership. Another hears: my opinion is welcome, but in the end I do what he decides. And “partnership” is just as slippery. One means complete equality of authority. Another means shared responsibility, while still holding that the husband has a distinct role.

slides.kicker: Ask for an example, every time
body: “What do I mean by headship? Give an example.” An ordinary-life example for each word, so you can see whether you mean the same thing.
slides.narration: So do not assume that using the same theological vocabulary means you have the same marriage in mind. And ask for an example, every time. “What do I mean by headship? Give an example.” “What do I mean by submission? Give an example.” Give an ordinary-life example for each word, so that you can see whether you mean the same thing.

list: If we strongly disagreed about moving, who makes the final decision?
Can either of us raise a serious objection without fear or punishment?
Which decisions need both our free agreement?
What happens when a decision turns out badly?
slides.narration: Then ask the questions that bring it down to earth. Suppose we strongly disagree about moving to another city. What actually happens? Who makes the final decision? What does consultation look like before that decision? Can either person raise a serious objection without fear or punishment? Which decisions require the free agreement of both people? Is either person expected to comply when conscience, safety, bodily autonomy or a major legal or financial commitment is involved? And what happens when the person who usually leads makes a decision that turns out badly? That last question is worth more than most of the theology, because it shows whether the arrangement includes any correction, or whether leadership means never being answerable.

slides.title: What am I assuming my partner will simply do, in our home, without ever having discussed it?
body: Take a moment before you go on.
slides.narration: Pause here. What am I assuming my partner will simply do, in our home, without ever having discussed it? Take a moment before you go on.

slides.title: An ordinary Tuesday, five years from now
body: Each describe it separately, morning to night: who does what, who decides what, where each of you is at four in the afternoon. Then exchange them.
slides.narration: Here is the best exercise I know, and I would put it ahead of an hour of theological discussion. Each of you describes, separately, an ordinary Tuesday five years from now. Morning to night. Who does what, who decides what, where each of you is at four in the afternoon. Then exchange them and read both before saying anything. It is remarkable how often two people who agree perfectly in principle describe two different Tuesdays.

slides.title: Bring it to understand, not to win
body: The moment Scripture becomes a weapon, disagreeing looks like disagreeing with God. That is leverage, not persuasion.
slides.narration: If you hold different theological positions, slow down. This is the room where our rule about Scripture as a weapon is tested hardest. Bring the passages that shape your conviction, but bring them to understand one another rather than to win. The moment Scripture becomes a weapon, the other person can no longer disagree with you without appearing to disagree with God. That is not persuasion. It is leverage.

chips: Explain your conviction without attacking the other’s
Which passages matter most, and how did you come to hold them?
What would this belief require of my spouse in everyday married life?
slides.narration: Take it in three steps. First, each explains their conviction without attacking the other’s: what do I believe Scripture teaches about husbands and wives, and why? The other listens as we learned in Lesson 5: a question first, repeat it back, then respond. Second: which passages or principles matter most to me here, and how did I come to hold them? Some find they inherited a position rather than examined one. That is not shameful. It is worth knowing. And third, the question that does the work: what would this belief actually require of my spouse in everyday married life? Often a couple finds that their disagreement is theological in language and practical in consequence. Sometimes it is not. One believes the husband holds final decision-making authority; the other believes significant decisions must always be mutually agreed. That is not a difference of emphasis, and you need to know it before the wedding.

slides.title: Not complementarian or egalitarian
body: This course will not tell either of you to change. Serious Christians have read the same Scriptures and reached different conclusions.
slides.narration: Here is where I stand. This course will not tell one of you to become complementarian, or the other to become egalitarian, and it will not settle that theological debate for you. These are convictions held by serious Christians who have read the same Scriptures carefully and reached different conclusions. You may seek guidance from a pastor who will explain Scripture carefully, represent your questions fairly and help you understand what each position would require in daily married life. What this course can do is help you examine Scripture honestly, understand what you believe and why, and decide whether you can build a marriage with integrity around those convictions.

slides.kicker: One thing I will say plainly
slides.note: Whatever position you hold, an arrangement in which one person cannot raise a concern, cannot disagree, or cannot be heard when something is wrong is not a faithful expression of marriage in Christ. Neither can be healthy where honesty is unsafe.
slides.narration: But one thing I will say plainly. Whatever position you hold, an arrangement in which one person cannot raise a concern, cannot disagree, or cannot be heard when something is wrong is not a faithful expression of marriage in Christ, whatever vocabulary is used to describe it. Complementarian marriages and egalitarian marriages can both be healthy. Neither can be healthy where honesty is unsafe.

slides.kicker: If one of you has never thought about it
slides.title: A conviction adopted to end a conversation is not a conviction
body: Give a real difference more than one evening. Speak to a pastor who will help you both think.
slides.narration: If you find one of you has never thought about it, do not let the one with the settled position simply install it. A conviction adopted to end a conversation is not a conviction. And if you find a genuinely different understanding of authority, give it more than one evening. Speak to a pastor, ideally one who will help you both think, not one who will simply confirm whichever of you already agrees with them. And be honest about whether either of you is hoping the other will come round after the wedding.

slides.title: About twenty minutes
body: Each writes a description of an ordinary Tuesday five years into your marriage. Do not compare notes.
slides.narration: Your step has two parts. First, separately, about twenty minutes. Each of you writes a description of an ordinary Tuesday five years into your marriage. Do not compare notes.

slides.title: 45 to 60 minutes
list: Where do our two Tuesdays differ, and what surprised us?
What do I mean by headship, submission, partnership and spiritual leadership?
If we strongly disagreed about a major decision, what would actually happen?
slides.narration: Then set aside 45 to 60 minutes, together, when neither of you is tired. Have your Lesson 2 rules in front of you. Exchange your Tuesdays, and read both before anyone speaks. Then work through three main questions. First: where do our two Tuesdays differ, and what surprised us? Second: what do I mean by headship, by submission, by partnership, and by spiritual leadership? Give an example of each. Third: if we strongly disagreed about a major decision, what would actually happen? Can either of us raise a serious objection without fear? Which decisions need both our free agreements? And how would we raise it if a decision turned out badly?

slides.title: Other conversations
body: Who does which tasks. What counts as a major decision. Test cases: a job in another city, leaving a church, one of you stopping work when a child arrives, lending a large sum to family.
slides.narration: The other conversations are worth having over the coming weeks: who does which tasks, what counts as a major decision, and the test cases, such as a job in another city, leaving a church, one of you stopping work when a child arrives, or lending a large sum to a family member. The Household Responsibilities Sheet can wait for another day.

slides.note: If at any point one person cannot refuse coercion, raise a concern, follow conscience, seek help or speak honestly without punishment, stop. Speak to someone outside the relationship.
slides.narration: If at any point one person cannot refuse coercion, raise a concern, follow conscience, seek help or speak honestly without punishment, stop. Whatever theology it is dressed in, that is the thing to stop for. Speak to someone outside the relationship.

body: Lord, thank You for Christ, who gave himself up for us. Teach us mutual care that protects each person’s dignity and voice. Keep us from using Your Word to silence one another. Give husbands hearts that serve, and give each of us the courage to speak and the humility to listen. Amen.
slides.narration:
Let me close with a short prayer.

Lord, thank You for Christ, who gave himself up for us. Teach us mutual care that protects each person’s dignity and voice. Keep us from using Your Word to silence one another. Give husbands hearts that serve, and give each of us the courage to speak and the humility to listen. Amen.

slides.narration: I’ll see you in Lesson 12.
